The local density of infectious tick vectors and the spatial velocity of a Lyme disease epidemic can both increase or decrease with increasing rates of juvenile tick attack on hosts.

the local and spatial dynamics of tick‐borne disease are determined by the interaction of density‐independent tick mortality, the rate at which juvenile ticks attack hosts, and the stage‐structured transmission of the disease.

the spatial spread of Lyme disease, which is caused by a tick-borne bacterium, Borrelia burgdorferi.
the spatial spread of vector-borne disease.

the rate of spread of an emerging disease depends on a complex interaction of biotic and abiotic factors that can be captured by our reaction–diffusion model.

we have developed a stage-structured model of Lyme disease transmission and used this model to study how the spatial dynamics of Lyme disease epidemics depend on the density-independent survival of the vector, the density-dependent survival of the vector (which is affected by competition between vector stages), and the rate of juvenile tick attack on mammalian hosts.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the rate at which a vector-borne disease advances spatially can be influenced by biotic factors that affect the vector's stage structure.
